Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I have failed in my most important role in life
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner', the appraisal 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' is clinically hard to reconcile because this trauma does not ordinarily involve other deaths or a mass-casualty context. The rest of the profile centers on partner violence, hypervigilance, and fragmented visual recall, so this item introduces a markedly different trauma scenario without support elsewhere in the selected items.

'Car sounds' is difficult to connect clinically to the rest of this profile for physical abuse by a romantic partner. The other trigger items and all threat, memory, and appraisal items center on interpersonal trauma, bodily alarm, betrayal, and fragmented terror-based recall. A car-sound trigger suggests a different trauma context unless there is supporting material elsewhere, so this item is the main coherence concern.

vignette: Vikram Patel had been forty when the altercation at home shifted the ground beneath him. He remembered the evening clearly: his wife, Maya, had raised her voice during a disagreement over household finances, and her hand had connected with his shoulder, followed by a sharp shove that sent him crashing against the granite kitchen island. What startled him most was the immediate physical collapse of his stomach, a wave of nausea that rose before he even registered the pain. The air thickened with the sharp, familiar scent of her gin and tonic, a smell that seemed to lock his chest in a vise. As she continued speaking, her words blurred into a stream of English and Gujarati, the syllables overlapping until they became an incomprehensible chatter that vibrated in his ears. He felt the danger surge through his limbs before his mind could name it, his muscles tensing, his breath shortening, entirely unmoored from the room’s quiet reality. In the weeks that followed, Vikram found himself living with a persistent, low-grade physical unease. Even on clear mornings, a sudden wave of illness would sweep through him, making him pause mid-stride or grip the edge of his drafting table at work. His sleep grew restless; he lay awake for hours, convinced he needed to stay alert, his body braced as though another movement might erupt from the darkness. When he finally drifted off, the event would surface in his mind not as a story, but as a series of static images. Each moment of the attack arrived as a snapshot—Maya’s raised arm, the glint of the gin glass, the sudden blur of her mixed-language speech—and holding the memory was like looking through a photographic album where the terror felt as immediate as the original moment. He had come to believe that his body knew danger sooner than his thoughts could catch up, and this continuous readiness left him jumpy, his shoulders lifting at the clatter of a dropped pen or the sudden call of his name. Over months, the habits settled into place. He began avoiding the kitchen, then gradually the living room, telling himself he needed quiet to focus on his blueprints. At his architectural firm, the collaborative studio became a place where he stood just out of the main circle, listening to colleagues weave their conversations, the overlapping voices sometimes triggering that same wave of physical malaise. He started double-checking his structural calculations, then triple-checking them, unable to trust that his judgment would hold. The avoidance carried tangible consequences: he missed several evening dinners with Maya, the silence between them growing heavier with each unshared meal, and he delayed signing off on a crucial residential project, certain that his hesitation masked a deeper failure. He had come to see himself as a husband who had failed his most important role, betrayed by the very person who had stood beside him when the impact first landed. His self-doubt lingered like a quiet companion, present during site walks and late-night drafting sessions, whispering that he might not navigate the next moment correctly. At forty-one, Vikram sat in the therapist’s office with his portfolio resting against his knees, his hands still resting lightly on the leather armrests as if ready to steady himself. He had finally sought help after a recent evening where the smell of a colleague’s post-meeting whiskey at a firm dinner, the overlapping chatter, and a sudden jolt of nausea had left him stepping out onto the pavement, certain he could not stay in the room. What frightened him most was not the physical pain or the sharp sounds, but the uncertainty of his own judgment and the fear that he had lost his place in his own life. He was hoping, quietly, to find a way to rest without bracing for the next impact, to trust his eyes and his hands again, and to step back into his home and his work without the constant, quiet vigilance.
